**Everything compiles.**  In 3.0.0 the compiler took the core of the language
and *declined a whole body* when it met something it did not handle — and a body
it declined ran on the tree-walker, all the way through.  Thirteen forms were
in that list: `do`, `guard`, `quasiquote`, `parameterize`, `define-values`,
`let-values`, `let*-values`, `case-lambda`, `delay`, `delay-force`,
`define-record-type`, `match` and `select`.  They are all compiled now, along
with `cond-expand`, `go`, and the macros a body defines.  **Nothing is left.**

```sh
goscheme script.scm                  # the whole file is bytecode now
goscheme -interp script.scm          # the tree-walker, for comparison
goscheme compile script.scm          # writes script.scmc
goscheme build script.scm            # a standalone executable of bytecode
```

### What made it possible

Two things, and the second is the interesting one.

Most of these forms *are* other forms.  A `do` loop is a `letrec` whose body is
guarded; a `let-values` is `call-with-values` around fresh temporaries; a
`` ` `` template is `cons` and `append`.  The interpreter already had those
expansions, so the compiler now calls the same functions (`doExpansion`,
`letValuesForm`, `EvalQuasiquote`) and compiles what they return.  One
definition, two execution paths, no chance of drift.

The rest need something at run time, and get it as a **compiled procedure handed
to a helper**: a `guard` compiles its clauses to a procedure of the condition
and its body to a thunk; `select` compiles each clause expression to a thunk and
a helper applies them in order and runs the same selection; `match` compiles the
guard and body of each clause and hands the patterns to the same matcher the
interpreter uses; `go` compiles its body to the thunk a thread runs.  The
matching, the selection and the handler are the interpreter's own code — only
the pieces around them became bytecode, so the two paths cannot disagree about
what a pattern matches or which clause wins.

A constant pool can name one of those helpers (`GSCM` format version 3, datum
tag 17), which a program can neither see nor rebind: a compiled `guard` must
reach its helper whatever the program has done to its own names.

### A macro defined in a body

This one needed new machinery.  The interpreter evaluates a transformer in the
environment where it is written; a compiled body has no environment — its
variables are slots.  The compiler now keeps a **shadow environment** beside
every scope: a real `Env` with the same names, whose values are never read.  It
exists so a mark on a template's identifier names a scope, that scope names a
block, and that block names the slot the variable lives in.  Hygiene comes out
the same as the interpreter's for every macro whose definition scope encloses
its use — including the R7RS suite's own `let-syntax` test, which is exactly
this case and which failed until the shadow environment existed.

### The bugs compiling them exposed

Compiling a form means the test suites finally *run* it, and five defects that
only the compiled path could have came out of that:

* `letrec` assigned each initializer as it was evaluated, which is `letrec*`.
  R7RS evaluates every initializer before assigning any of them.
* a binding form that names the same variable twice is an error, and the
  compiler said nothing.
* an internal definition in a `let`, `let*` or `letrec` body was compiled as a
  *global* definition, so a name that was already global resolved to the global
  before the definition had run.
* `case`'s `(else => proc)` compiled as two body expressions, so the procedure
  was returned instead of applied.
* a macro that defines a macro (the R7RS suite's `be-like-begin1`) used the
  macro before the compiler knew it, and `=>` bound as a local variable was
  still treated as the auxiliary keyword.

Each has a test.  The differential corpus is 64 programs run **three ways** —
compiled, compiled-to-bytes-and-back, and interpreted — and the R7RS reference
suite and every extension suite run **twice**, once per path.

### Faster, and measured

The same twelve-workload panel as 3.0.0, best of three runs, each figure
including building the machine and compiling the program:

| | bytecode | tree-walker | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lists` | 67.7 ms | 348.8 ms | **5.15×** |
| `locals` | 57.7 ms | 217.8 ms | **3.78×** |
| `mini-eval` | 16.4 ms | 56.9 ms | **3.48×** |
| `higher-order` | 16.9 ms | 58.6 ms | **3.47×** |
| `vectors` | 27.5 ms | 95.5 ms | **3.47×** |
| `sort` | 7.8 ms | 26.6 ms | **3.40×** |
| `tail-loop` | 48.2 ms | 158.2 ms | **3.28×** |
| `globals` | 56.0 ms | 179.5 ms | **3.21×** |
| `fib` | 5.6 ms | 13.7 ms | **2.44×** |
| `callcc` | 8.7 ms | 21.1 ms | **2.43×** |
| `closures` | 13.5 ms | 31.0 ms | **2.29×** |
| `strings` | 6.1 ms | 8.0 ms | **1.31×** |

Geometric mean **3.0×**, **82% fewer bytes allocated** — unchanged from 3.0.0,
because the panel's programs were already compiling.  What changed is
everything else: in this repository every ordinary top-level form of every
example and every test suite is now bytecode, and **no source chunk is left
except the ones that have to be** — an `import`, a `define-syntax` at the top
level, an `include` — which are run while compiling and kept so that loading
the file performs them again.

### Also in this release

* The bytecode format is documented in full: [docs/bytecode-internals.md](../docs/bytecode-internals.md) —
  the header, the encodings, the three chunk kinds, the seventeen datum tags,
  the twenty-three instructions with their stack effects, what the machine does
  when it runs a call, and the measurements.  `docs/bytecode.md` remains the
  overview.
* The reader takes `\NNN`, `\e` and `\xHH` without the semicolon, so
  `"\033[31m"` is what it looks like.
* A bracketed paste is inserted at the cursor, not at the end of the line.
* Ctrl-C abandons a half-written expression in the REPL instead of leaving it
  to be finished.
* `goscheme compile` and `goscheme build` say nothing when they succeed.
